Photograph: James Ross/AAP BHP At least 109 BHP workers sexually harassed colleagues in a single year, mining company says Further 104 allegations not investigated due to ‘insufficient information or the wishes of the impacted person’, according to annual report Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jonathan Barrett Business editor Tue 18 Aug 2026 00.46 EDT Last modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 02.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 100 workers at BHP lost their jobs, or resigned, during the last financial year after sexually harassing colleagues, which included numerous instances of indecent touching, stalking and grooming. The harassment cases, disclosed in the mining giant’s annual report on Tuesday, come during a period of heightened scrutiny of remote work sites, where female workers across the industry have raised allegations of systemic sexual harassment, violence and retaliation. Australia’s largest aluminium smelter to run on renewables by 2033 after Rio Tinto strikes $2.5bn taxpayer bailout deal Read more BHP, the world’s biggest miner, has large iron ore and copper operations in Australia, and North and South America. The miner disclosed that 109 workers lost their jobs, or resigned, in 2025-26, following 113 confirmed reports of sexual harassment. It was the highest number of confirmed reports since 2023. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email BHP said that allegations are investigated by an ethics team independent from operations. The company does not provide a geographic breakdown of the confirmed sexual harassment cases. A further 104 reports of sexual harassment were not investigated “due to insufficient information or the wishes of the impacted person”. The majority of confirmed instances involved indecent touching, stalking, grooming and sexually aggressive comments and jokes. Past parliamentary inquiries and reports by the office of the sex discrimination commissioner have found cultures of sexual assault, sexism, bullying and racism across the mining industry, especially at remote projects where workers stay for weeks at a time. There are three separate class actions in the courts against BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue alleging widespread sexual harassment, sexual violence and sex discrimination at work sites. The class actions, filed by law firm JGA Saddler, allege that “most women, if not all” working on remote sites have suffered some form of sexual harassment or sex discrimination. BHP also disclosed that 22 people responsible for racial harassment had their employment terminated, or resigned, last financial year. Jodie Fox, an employment lawyer who specialises in workplace investigations, said mining projects have a number of risk factors for women, including isolated workplaces, hierarchical structures and a gender imbalance. “In a lot of these places, the workplace and your place of accommodation and your place of socialising are all effectively in the one place,” said Fox, a director at Worklogic. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “You’ve got a perfect storm of risk for sexual harassment.” She said employers have a duty to prevent and eliminate sexual harassment where possible. Renewables demand On Tuesday, BHP declared a bumper US$9.8bn (A$13.8bn) annual net profit, up 9%, and its highest dividend in four years, in a result boosted by surging copper prices. Copper, which plays a central role in power grids, is widely viewed as the metal that underpins the fast-growing renewable energy industry, and is an important component for AI datacentres. Prices for the red metal have climbed to record highs this year, surpassing US$14,000 per metric ton. BHP expects global copper demand to grow to more than 50m metric tons per year by 2050, from 34m this year, and foresees a supply crunch. BHP said on Tuesday that copper was the “engine that is driving BHP’s growth”, a description that used to be applied to the company’s still-robust iron ore operations. The miner announced a US99c (A$1.39) final dividend, bringing total dividends for the year to US$1.72 (A$2.42) a share, up almost 60% on last year. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/fou.text: The Budapest Times Four years frozen, 4.2 billion euros unlocked — but at what cost? The conditionality procedure launched against Hungary concluded on Tuesday, releasing 4.2 billion euros in EU funds, with the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes set to become accessible again to Hungarian students and researchers. Hungary’s Permanent Representation to the European Union informed the public on its social media page that the decision by the Council of the European Union opens the way for full access to the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes. According to the notice, member states decided by consensus to close the conditionality procedure against Hungary. “As a result of the decision, our country will once again have access to 4.2 billion euros from cohesion funds, and the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes will become available to all Hungarian universities. The decision is an important achievement for Hungary, as it brings to a close a process lasting more than four years, thanks to the large-scale anti-corruption package of measures implemented in recent months, which addressed all previous concerns raised by the European Commission and the Council of the European Union,” the statement read. The conditionality mechanism linked to the rule of law, which entered into force on 1 January 2021, serves to protect the EU budget and the financial interests of the Union against violations of the principles of the rule of law. Under the mechanism, member states can only fully access EU funds if they respect fundamental rule-of-law values in their operations, including the independence of the judiciary, effective action against corruption, and the integrity of public procurement. The procedure was first applied by the Council of the European Union against Hungary, under which 55 percent of the budgetary commitments of three Hungarian cohesion programmes were frozen due to shortcomings in the public procurement system, corruption risks, and concerns related to the independence of the judiciary. The condition for releasing the frozen amounts was the complete and verified fulfilment of the so-called super-milestones and rule-of-law conditions. At the end of September, the European Commission announced that it had found the reforms introduced by the new Hungarian government to have yielded results: “Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the financial interests of the Union.” It then proposed to the Council of the European Union that 4.2 billion euros in cohesion funds be released for Hungary, and that the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes be made available again to Hungarian students and researchers. Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, welcomed the Council’s decision on X, highlighting that it marked — as she emphasised — the beginning of a new chapter for both Hungary and Europe. Viktor Weisz, a Member of the European Parliament for Tisza Párt, stressed in a statement sent to MTI that the EU Council’s decision proves that lost European opportunities can be regained through meaningful reforms and by strengthening the rule of law and transparency. Hungarian young people must not pay the price for political decisions. Erasmus+ is not a privilege but a right — an opportunity to learn, to grow, and to discover Europe, he stressed. “We are working to ensure that these opportunities are available to every young Hungarian,” the Tisza Párt MEP added. According to a statement from the European Commission, following the decision, Michael McGrath, the Commissioner responsible for democracy, justice, and the rule of law, declared: “this decision also clearly signals that Hungary has unambiguously returned to the European path.” He recalled that over the past months, the new Hungarian government had made significant progress in restoring the rule of law and had reversed several decisions made by the previous government. The decision shows that Hungary’s efforts to restore the rule of law are bearing fruit, he stated. Respect for the rule of law is a fundamental condition for access to EU funds, the EU Commissioner added in his statement.
